Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for how you could use the two tools you described to place a “burger + fries” order at McDonald’s. (Everything is written in plain English – you’ll replace the placeholders with real values once you’ve found the actual API.) --- ## 1. Find the right API | What you do | Why it matters | How to do it with the “search” tool | |-------------|----------------|-------------------------------------| | **Search the web for McDonald’s ordering APIs** | McDonald’s doesn’t publish a public API for customers, but many restaurants expose a private API that the mobile app uses. You’ll need the exact endpoint, auth method, and payload schema. | `search("McDonald's ordering API burger fries")` | | **Look for third‑party delivery APIs** | If McDonald’s has no public API, you can order through a delivery partner (Uber Eats, DoorDash, Grubhub, etc.). Those partners expose documented APIs. | `search("Uber Eats order API burger fries")` | | **Collect documentation** | You’ll need to know:
• Base URL
• Authentication (OAuth2, API key, JWT, etc.)
• Required headers
• Request body format (JSON, form‑data)
• Menu item IDs for “burger” and “fries”
• Location / pickup address
• Payment token | `search("Uber Eats API docs")` | > **Tip:** If you find a public Swagger/OpenAPI spec, you can copy the exact request body template. --- ## 2. Prepare authentication | What you do | Why it matters | How to do it | |-------------|----------------|--------------| | **Obtain an access token** | Most APIs require a bearer token. You’ll usually get it by sending a login request with a username/password or by exchanging a refresh token. | `execute("POST https://api.ubereats.com/v1/auth/login\n{ \"email\": \"you@example.com\", \"password\": \"••••••\" }")` | | **Store the token** | Keep it in a variable for subsequent calls. | `token = ` | | **Set the Authorization header** | Every request must include `Authorization: Bearer `. | `headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Content-Type": "application/json" }` | --- ## 3. Build the order payload | What you do | Why it matters | How to do it | |-------------|----------------|--------------| | **Find menu item IDs** | The API expects numeric IDs, not human‑readable names. | `search("McDonald's menu item ID burger")` → e.g. `burger_id = 12345` | | **Create the JSON body** | Include quantity, any customizations, delivery address, and payment method. | ```json\n{\n "items": [\n { "id": 12345, "quantity": 1 },\n { "id": 67890, "quantity": 1 }\n ],\n "delivery_address": {\n "street": "123 Main St",\n "city": "Anytown",\n "zip": "12345"\n },\n "payment_method": {\n "type": "card",\n "token": ""\n }\n}\n``` | > **Note:** If you’re using a delivery partner, the payload will differ slightly (e.g., `restaurant_id`, `delivery_fee`, etc.). --- ## 4. Execute the order | What you do | Why it matters | How to do it | |-------------|----------------|--------------| | **Send the POST request** | This is the actual “order” call. | ```python\nresponse = execute(\n url="https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders",\n method="POST",\n headers=headers,\n body=order_json\n)\n``` | | **Check the response** | Look for `status: success` and an `order_id`. | `if response.status == "success": print("Order placed! ID:", response.order_id)` | | **Handle errors** | If the API returns 4xx/5xx, log the message and retry if appropriate. | `else: print("Error:", response.error_message)` | --- ## 5. Optional post‑order steps | What you do | Why it matters | How to do it | |-------------|----------------|--------------| | **Track the order** | Get real‑time status (preparing, out for delivery). | `GET https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders//status` | | **Cancel the order** | If you change your mind. | `DELETE https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders/` | | **Add a tip** | Tip the delivery driver. | `PATCH https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders/\n{ "tip": 5 }` | | **Apply a promo code** | Get a discount. | `PATCH https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders/\n{ "promo_code": "SAVE10" }` | --- ## 6. Wrap it up in a script ```python def order_burger_and_fries(): # 1. Authenticate auth_resp = execute( url="https://api.ubereats.com/v1/auth/login", method="POST", body={"email": "you@example.com", "password": "••••••"} ) token = auth_resp.access_token headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", "Content-Type": "application/json"} # 2. Build payload payload = { "items": [ {"id": 12345, "quantity": 1}, # burger {"id": 67890, "quantity": 1} # fries ], "delivery_address": { "street": "123 Main St", "city": "Anytown", "zip": "12345" }, "payment_method": {"type": "card", "token": ""} } # 3. Place order order_resp = execute( url="https://api.ubereats.com/v1/orders", method="POST", headers=headers, body=payload ) if order_resp.status == "success": print(f"Order placed! ID: {order_resp.order_id}") else: print(f"Order failed: {order_resp.error_message}") # Run the function order_burger_and_fries() ``` --- ### Bottom line 1. **Search** for the correct API endpoint and documentation. 2. **Authenticate** and store the bearer token. 3. **Build** the JSON payload with the correct item IDs, quantity, address, and payment token. 4. **Execute** the POST request via the “execute API call” tool. 5. **Handle** the response (success, error, tracking, etc.). If McDonald’s itself doesn’t expose a public API, swap the base URL and payload to match a delivery partner’s API (Uber Eats, DoorDash, etc.). The same workflow applies—just the endpoint URLs and field names change.
